chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Malik ibn Atiyya, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira died, so Umm Salama said to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family): 'The family of al-Mughira have established a lamentation, so I will go to them.' He permitted her, so she wore her clothes and prepared herself, and from her beauty she was like a fairy. Whenever she stood up and let down her hair, it covered her body, and she tied her ornaments at its ends.

She eulogized her cousin in front of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), saying: 'I announce the death of Al-Walid ibn Al-Walid, Abu Al-Walid, the youth of the clan, the protector of the reality, the glorious one who ascends in seeking the frequent one. He was a rain in the years, a spring of abundant water, and a provision.'
The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) did not object to that from her, nor did he say anything.

key_terms.نَدَبَ: To eulogize or recite poetry in praise

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on women participating in lamentation and eulogy according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* establishes the permissibility of *manah* (lamentation) for women, specifically highlighting Umm Salama’s eulogy of Al-Walid ibn Al-Mughira as a precedent for expressive mourning. The Prophet’s silence indicates his approval of her poetic recitation and physical demeanor, reinforcing the Shia scholarly view that women’s mourning rituals are distinct from men’s and culturally valid. It underscores the social legitimacy of public grief and poetic expression within the early Islamic community.
